card: The first question to ask of any environmental number, and the one most often skipped.

frame.alt: Fourteen open nature journals laid out in rows on a dark cloth, each spread pairing a real pressed leaf or seed pod with a painted study of the same leaf beside it

answer: A measured number came from an instrument pointed at the thing. A modelled number came from a calculation about the thing. Both can be right and both can be wrong, but they fail in different ways and they cannot be compared as though they were the same kind of claim. Every figure on this site carries which of the two it is, on the rule beneath it.
explainLead: The distinction is useful because it tells you what to be suspicious of.
explain: A measurement fails at the instrument. It can be miscalibrated, saturated, obstructed, or reporting its own floor rather than a real value. It describes one point in space at one moment, and nothing else. When CPCB's dissolved-oxygen figure reads 0.3 mg/L at four Delhi stations, that is the floor the method reports — the true value is at or below it, and printing "0.0" would be an invention.

A model fails at its assumptions. A source-apportionment split, an emissions inventory, a death toll attributed to a pollutant and a satellite product that infers a quantity from radiance are all model outputs. They can cover a whole country and a whole year, which no instrument can, and they inherit every uncertainty in their inputs.

Neither is superior. A national figure for anything is almost always modelled, because measuring a nation is not possible. A street-level figure is almost always measured, because modelling a street is not reliable. Asking which one you are holding tells you what it can be used for.

defs.d: Produced by an instrument or a direct count. Fails locally and sharply.
Produced by calculation from other quantities. Fails globally and softly.
A model that assimilates historical observations to produce a consistent gridded record. Not a measurement, and not a free invention either — the honest description is modelled.

standard.head: How this site marks the difference
standard.lead: Every figure carries a rule beneath it: solid for counted or measured, dotted for modelled. It is on the figure, not in a footnote.

after: There is no limit on this page to break. The rule here is editorial, not legal: if you quote a number from this site, quote the kind with it. A modelled figure presented as a measurement is the most common way an honest number becomes a false claim.

readLead: Four questions that separate the two in almost every case.
measure: What produced this number? An instrument, a count, or a calculation. If a source does not say, treat it as modelled until it does.
What would have to be true for it to be wrong? For a measurement: a broken sensor, a bad sample, a saturated reading. For a model: a wrong assumption applied uniformly, which is far harder to notice.
What is its coverage? Measurements are sparse and precise. Models are complete and uncertain. A figure that is both complete and precise is worth a second look.
Is it being compared with the other kind? A modelled national estimate set against a measured city reading is not a comparison, even when both are correct.
cannot: The distinction cannot tell you which number is closer to the truth. It tells you how each one is likely to be wrong.
It cannot be applied to a figure whose provenance is not published — which is itself the finding.
It does not settle disagreements between two models, which is a separate problem: see source apportionment.
It says nothing about whether the thing measured was the right thing to measure.
